## Introduction

Two-dimensional (2D) materials have extraordinary characteristics that offer promising new approaches for science and technology. Electrons in graphene can move ballistically through a sheet, even though it is only a single atom thick (Geim & Novoselov 2007, Zhang et al. 2005). And transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) materials can be cleaved into 2D flakes of all types – metals, semiconductors, insulators, magnetic materials, and superconductors (Wang et al. 2012, Lee et al. 2013, Manzeli et al. 2017). To benefit from these discoveries, we need to understand the science and transform 2D materials into useful new devices and systems. With a TEM, we have studied how atomic scale graphene structures evolve in time.  By imaging electron motion with our cooled scanning probe microscope (SPM), we have explored ballistic transport of electrons in graphene as well as electron motion in MoS2.

Graphene is only one atom thick but is extremely strong, creating the opportunity to fabricate atomic scale structures in the lateral direction.  Using an atomic resolution TEM, we discovered that a suspended sheet of graphene can be shaped by a Si impurity atom on its surface that acts like a chisel to open up apertures, one atom at a time.  The electrons in the TEM provides both the chiseling energy and the ability to image the results (Wang et al. 2014).

Electrons and holes in graphene form a new type of electronic system with conical conduction and valence bands that meet at the Dirac point, with no energy gap (Geim and Novoselov 2007, Tan et al. 2007). For moderate densities, the carriers form a Fermi liquid with ballistic transport over micron-scale distances.  Using a cooled SPM (see below) we imaged the cyclotron orbit of electrons in graphene (Bhandari et al. 2016).  In the magnetic focusing regime, electrons leaving a point contact circle around and exit through a second point contact when the cyclotron diameter is equal to the contact spacing.  The paths of electrons are focused - they enter at different angles but converge again at the exit contact.  When the SPM tip knocks an electron out of its orbit, an imaging signal is created.

The ballistic motion of carriers in graphene opens the way for ballistic devices that manipulate beams of electrons and holes.  Our collaborator Gil-Ho Lee, in Philip Kim's group, created a collimating contact by placing zig-zag absorbers on either side of entering electrons.  We used our cooled SPM to image the beam and determine its 9-degree halfwidth (Bhandari et al. 2018b). By changing the gate voltage, we also created a collimated beam of holes (Bhandari et al. 2020a), opening the way for colliding beams.

Coherent beams of carriers are desirable for quantum information processing.  Via Andreev reflection, superconducting contacts can covert Cooper pairs to ingoing and outgoing electrons and holes.  Using our cooled SPM, we were able to image Andreev reflection from a superconducting contact on a graphene device (Bhandari et al. 2020b).  Magnetic focusing was used to create an incoming beam of electrons and an outgoing beam of holes, detected by a third point contact.  The images show a clear transition from normal reflection above the superconducting transition temperature to Andreev reflection as the device is cooled.

Transition metal dichalcogenides offer a wide array of materials that can be exfoliated into ultrathin 2D sheets.  A cooled SPM can be used to detect quantum dots as well as to image electron flow.  The tip charge capacitively couples to electrons on the dot, acting as a gate to tune the dot conductance.  Coulomb blockade peaks appear as a bullseye pattern in an SPM image as the tip is raster scanned above the dot.  We used this approach to detect quantum dots in a MoS2 channel as the carrier density was reduced and electrons pooled in low energy points (Bhandari et al. 2018a).

Through our DOE supported research, cooled SPM imaging has proven to be a very useful tool to uncover the motion of electrons and holes in graphene and MoS2.

Research Accomplishments

Chiseling Atomic Structures in Graphene using a Single Atom Catalyst -

Fabricating functional atomic scale structures in graphene is an important goal.  We have shown that a single Si adatom acts as an atomic chisel that catalyzes the removal of C atoms when it is illuminated by a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM).  The Si atom chisels single C atoms off of the graphene sheet, one after the other, but is not removed itself (Wang et al. 2014).  Theoretical simulations agree very well with the HRTEM images and show that the Si adatom dramatically increases the cross section for C atom removal.

*Figure 1 shows (top) HRTEM images (80 keV electron beam) of a suspended single layer graphene sheet with (bottom) theoretical simulations; these images demonstrate the catalytic process. Small silicon oxide nanoparticles on the graphene sheet dissociate into Si and O atoms, which are identified using electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS).  The Si atoms move rapidly over clean graphene, but stick to defects and edges.  The sequence of images in Fig. 1 shows that Si atoms initially group together, then open up an atomic-scale pore by zipping around the edge, removing C atoms one at a time.  The pore opening process can be stopped at any time by turning off the TEM beam.*

Low-Temperature Scanning Capacitance Probe for Imaging Electrons

We designed and implemented a cooled scanning capacitance probe that operates at liquid He temperatures to image electrons in two dimensional materials (Bhandari and Westervelt 2014).  The conducting tip of a scanned probe microscope is held above the nanoscale structure, and an applied tip-to-sample voltage creates an image charge that is measured by a cooled charge amplifier adjacent to the tip. The circuit, shown in Fig. 3 is based on a low-capacitance, high-electronmobility transistor. The input is a capacitance bridge formed by a low capacitance pinched-off HEMT transistor and tip-sample capacitance.  We achieved a low noise level (0.13 e/√Hz) and high spatial resolution (100 nm) for this technique, which promises to be a useful tool to study electronic in two dimensional materials without the need for electrical leads.

Imaging Andreev Reflection in Graphene from a Superconducting Contact

To create an interacting quantum system to process qubits, we need to find ways to transfer quantum information from one location to another. Coherent channels can be introduced into graphene from a superconductor by Andreev reflection (Andreev 1964, Beenakker 2008, Allen et al. 2016, Lee et al. 2017). An electron passing into a superconducting contact is reflected as a hole, while a Cooper pair is transmitted into the superconductor. Andreev reflection provides a microscopic picture of the superconducting proximity effect for normal conductors, and the operation of Josephson junctions.

To visualize the flow of electrons and holes during Andreev reflection (Bhandari et al. 2019a), we used a liquid-He cooled Scanning Probe Microscope (SPM). The SPM images ballistic paths of electrons by deflecting their trajectories and displaying the resulting change in conductance (Topinka et al. 2000). To define the trajectories of electrons and holes from a contact, we used magnetic focusing to bring the paths together at a second contact located a cyclotron diameter away. Our previous research has imaged the cyclotron orbits of electrons for a two-dimensional electron gas in graphene (Bhandari et al. 2016) and in a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostruture (Aidala et al. 2007). The graphene sample, shown in Figs. 6(c) and 6(f)), has three NbN superconducting contacts S2, S3 and S4 along the bottom side. At B = 0.13 T, electrons flow along cyclotron orbits between the two outer contacts S2 and S4 as shown in Fig. 6(a). When the field is doubled, Andreev refection occurs, as shown in Fig. 6(d): electron cyclotron orbits from S2 that hit the center superconducting contact S3 are Andreev-reflected as holes, which head for the collecting

Imaging Electron and Hole Beams from Collimating Contacts in Graphene

The ballistic travel of electrons and holes in graphene over distances greater than the device size opens the way for new types of ballistic electronics. To explore these opportunities, we developed collimating contacts that inject a narrow beam of electrons (Bhandari et al. 2018b) or holes (Bhandari et al. 2019b) into graphene; an SEM image of the device is shown in Fig. 2(a). A ray-tracing schematic diagram in Fig. 2(b) shows how the collimating contact works. Zigzag shaped side contacts absorb carriers entering at wide angles from the end contact, producing a narrow beam that enters the sample.

It is interesting to consider graphene devices that have two complimentary ballistic beams of carriers – one beam of electrons and one of holes – that can collide and interact. We created a hole beam in the graphene device shown in Fig. 7(a) by moving the Fermi energy into the valence band with a back gate (Bhandari et al. 2019b). Figure 9 shows a series of SPM images of a beam of holes passing from the zigzag collimating contact 1 on top to the receiving contact 3 on bottom of the device vs. n and B. The blue color in the images indicates that the SPM tip attracts holes and focuses them onto the receiving contact, while the electrons in Fig. 8 are repelled. As the B field is increased, the hole beam in Fig. 9 disappears, when the paths are bent along cyclotron orbits.

The interaction of complimentary beams of electrons and holes in graphene is particularly interesting when the Fermi energy is at the Dirac point, where the charge density drops to zero, but the conductivity remains finite ~ 4e2/h.  Electrons and holes are both present and strongly interact to form a Dirac fluid, but their total charge cancels. We plan to explore transport in this regime in our proposed work, as well as enhanced electron-electron collisions at higher densities and temperatures that create hydrodynamic flow.

Imaging Quantum Dots formed in a MoS2 Channel

Like graphite, molybdenum disulfide MoS2 can be separated into 2D materials with only a few quantum layers. Unlike graphene, MoS2 is a semiconductor with an energy gap and separate conduction and valence bands. Its devices are photosensitive, and their conductance can be switched with a gate. For high quality, MoS2 sheets should have high mobility and uniformity.

We have used our cooled SPM to test the uniformity of few layer MoS2 sheets, as the electron density was reduced to zero, as shown in Fig. 10 (Bhandari et al. 2018a).  As the density is reduced, electrons pool in the low spots of the background potential, creating small quantum dots. The SPM tip acts as a movable gate that tunes the number of electrons, creating a bullseye pattern of Coulomb conductance peaks that locate the dot and determine its size. As the density is increased, a second dot appears. Previously, we used this technique to test the uniformity of InAs nanowires (Bleszynski et al. 2017).

Our SPM images of quantum dots in MoS2 as the carrier density approaches zero, provide a detailed view of the background potential of the substrate. They can also be used to evaluate the uniformity of CVD grown layers of MoS2.and other transition metal dichalcogenide materials.

Imaging Universal Conductance Fluctuations and Weak Localization in Graphene

Using a liquid He cooled scanning probe microscope, we imaged Universal Conductance Fluctuations (UCF) (Berezovksy et al. 2010) and Weak Localizatiion (Berezovsky and Westervelt 2010) for electron waves passing through the two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) in a single atomic layer of graphene.  A conducting tip creates a movable scatterer in the graphene 2DEG below - theory predicts that one additional scatter completely rearranges the interference patterns that create UCF - so scanning the scatter across the area shows both the UCF amplitude (~ e2/h) and the characteristic spatial size, predicted to be half the Fermi wavelength F.  The SPM conductance image shows both effects: conductance fluctuations ~ e2/h over characteristic lengths ~ F/2.  These images repeat accurately over times as long as ~ 1 hr, demonstrating that the pattern is not created by random noise, but by reproducible interference between quantum waves bouncing off fixed scatterers.

Conductance fluctuations were also tested in a perpendicular magnetic field.  As the magnitude B was varied, the fluctuation patterns changed as additional phase is added to interfering loops.  The correlation clearly defines a characteristic magnetic field change Bc, which corresponds to a spatial coherence length Lf ~ 500 nm, comparable to the sample size.

Coaxial and Triaxial SPM Tips as Tweezers for Nanoscale Particles

A coaxial tip can act as a tweezer for small particles, using positive dielectrophoresis to pick and place small items, by switching the voltage on the inner conductor on and off (Brown, Aguilar and Westervelt 2011).  While assembly in the initial work occurred at the microscale, this process could be pushed to the nanoscale by using a finer coaxial tip.  We also used coaxial SPM tips to image dielectric objects by sensing the dielectrophoretic force between the coaxial tip and the objects (Brown, Berezovsky, and Westervelt 2011).  The combined ability to image small objects and to perform pick and place assembly using the same coaxial tip could prove to be very useful in the assembly of stacked atomically layered material structures and devices.

A triaxial tip is shown in Fig. 12.  It consists of a conducting core, surrounded by an inner shell, and a grounded outer shell, separated by insulating layers. By applying voltages of opposing sign to the core and inner shell, a zero in the electric field profile can be produced away from the surface of the triaxial tip.  By varying the core and inner shell voltages the trap

In addition, the trap is located at distances ~100 nm away from the tip, allowing one to capacitive probe structures below with nanoscale resolution.

To sharpen the tip potential and reduce the broad background produced by an unshielded tip, we have developed coaxial and triaxial SPM tips (Brown, Aguilar and Westervelt 2010, Brown, Berezovsky and Westervelt 2011, Brown and Westervelt 2011).  A coaxial tip consists of a conducting core surrounded by a grounded shell, separated by an insulating layer (Figs. 11a, 11b).  The outer shell acts as a shield that confines electric field lines to the end of the tip, changing the field distribution from monopole to dipole, and sharpening its spatial

distribution (Fig. 11c).

We developed a way to actuate SPM cantilevers using a capacitor fabricated along one side (Brown, Yang, and Westervelt 2012).  When a voltage is applied across the capacitor plates, they attract, bending the cantilever in that direction.  Despite its simplicity, this approach can be very effective, providing sufficient force to carry out typical SPM experiments.  It is particularly suited to the actuation of high frequency cantilevers, with resonant frequencies above 1 MHz, because the capacitor directly actuates the fundamental mode of oscillation.  By contrast, an external piezoelectric actuator actuated unwanted external modes.

High Spatial Resolution Kelvin Probe Microscopy

Kelvin probe microscopy measures the work function of a material, the energy required to remove an electron.  Kelvin probe images can be very useful for spatially structured materials, because they uncover the energies associated with interfaces and different structural conditions. One can do Kelvin probe imaging with an AFM tip by adjusting the tip voltage to zero the contact potential between the tip and the material below. For an unshielded tip one faces the difficulty that the resolution is limited by the spatial profile of the electric field from the tip.

We have developed a high-resolution Kelvin probe microscope based on a coaxial AFM tip (Brown, Satzinger and Westervelt, 2012, Satzinger, Brown and Westervelt 2012).  The coaxial shield sharpens the electric field profile, limiting the sensitivity to the material immediately below the tip.  By considering the two tip electrodes and the material, one can properly zero the contact potential to image the local work function of the material.  These high-resolution Kelvin probes could prove to be very useful in the characterization of stacked atomic layer structures, and MBE grown TI materials in the proposed research.
